'''Jay Kazuo Kochi''' (高知 和夫, ''Kōchi Kazuo'', 1927–2008) was an American physical organometallic chemist who held lectureship at [[Harvard University]], and faculty positions at Case Institute of Technology, 1962–1969, (now [[Case Western Reserve University]]), [[Indiana University]], 1969 to 1984, and the [[University of Houston]], 1984 to 2008.<ref name=inmemoriam/>

==Early life and education==
Kochi was born to Japanese immigrant parents on May 17, 1927, in Los Angeles, California, where he and his family had lived until he and his family were imprisoned at the [[Gila River War Relocation Center]] in 1942 just after the United States entered the Second World War and [[Executive Order 9066]] was signed.<ref name=inmemoriam/> After the war, Kochi and his family returned to California and Kochi later attended UCLA.<ref name="uhlib">{{cite web |url=https://weblogs.lib.uh.edu/speccol/2016/07/13/introducing-the-professor-jay-k-kochi-papers/ |title=Introducing the Professor Jay K. Kochi Papers |date=July 13, 2016 |first=Gregory |last=Yerke |work=University of Houston Libraries}}</ref>

Kochi received his [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] in 1949 and his Ph.D. at [[Iowa State University]] in 1952 with [[George S. Hammond]] and [[Henry Gilman]] as advisors.<ref name="thesis-kochi-1952">{{cite thesis |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/302077436 |title=The application of the Hammett equation to the solvolysis of benzyl tosylates |date=1952 |publisher=[[Iowa State University]] |type=Ph.D. |last=Kochi |first=Jay Kazuo |id={{ProQuest|302077436 }}|url-access=subscription  |oclc=908156744}}</ref> He then spent short stints at Harvard University, Cambridge University, Shell Development Co., Case Institute of Technology (now Case Western Reserve University), and Indiana University. For the majority of his faculty career, however, he was located at the [[University of Houston]], where he was Welch Professor.

==Research==
Kochi's research examined the interactions of electron donors and acceptors.  One topic of his study was the nitration of benzene to give [[nitrobenzene]]. Kochi's work showed that this reaction proceeds via a complex between [[benzene]] (the donor) and [[nitrosonium]] ion (the acceptor).<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1021/ar700256a| pmid = 18380446| title = Fresh Look at Electron-Transfer Mechanisms via the Donor/Acceptor Bindings in the Critical Encounter Complex| journal = Accounts of Chemical Research| volume = 41| issue = 5| pages = 641–53| year = 2008| last1 = Rosokha | first1 = S. V. | last2 = Kochi | first2 = J. K. }}</ref>  He also contributed to many aspects of [[organometallic chemistry]], including the discovery of Cu, Fe, and Ag-catalyzed cross-coupling processes (which preceded the discovery of the better known Pd and Ni-catalyzed versions),<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=TAMURA|first1=M.|last2=KOCHI|first2=J.|date=1971|title=Coupling of Grignard Reagents with Organic Halides|journal=Synthesis|language=en|volume=1971|issue=6|pages=303–305|doi=10.1055/s-1971-35043|s2cid=97706338 |issn=0039-7881}}</ref> as well as several metal-catalyzed oxidative processes.<ref name=MetalCatalyzedOxidations>{{cite book | last1=Sheldon | first1=Roger | last2=Kochi | first2=Jay | title=Metal-catalyzed oxidations of organic compounds : mechanistic principles and synthetic methodology including biochemical processes | publisher=Academic Press | location=New York | year=1981 | isbn=978-0-12-639380-4 | url-access=registration | url=https://archive.org/details/metalcatalyzedox0000shel }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book| doi = 10.1016/B978-0-12-639380-4.50007-5| chapter = Introduction to Metal-Catalyzed Oxidations| title = Metal-catalyzed Oxidations of Organic Compounds| pages = [https://archive.org/details/metalcatalyzedox0000shel/page/1 1]| year = 1981| last1 = Sheldon| first1 = R. A.| author-link1 = Roger A. Sheldon| last2 = Kochi| first2 = J. Y. K.| author-link2 = Jay Kochi| isbn = 9780126393804| chapter-url = https://archive.org/details/metalcatalyzedox0000shel/page/1}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1021/ja00269a029| title = Epoxidation of olefins with cationic (salen)manganese(III) complexes. The modulation of catalytic activity by substituents| journal = Journal of the American Chemical Society| volume = 108| issue = 9| pages = 2309–20| year = 1986| last1 = Srinivasan | first1 = K.| last2 = Michaud | first2 = P.| last3 = Kochi | first3 = J. K. | pmid=22175576| bibcode = 1986JAChS.108.2309S}}</ref>  At the time, these results were largely ignored by the synthetic organic chemistry community.  Many decades later, interest in [[base metal]] catalysis sparked significant efforts to further develop cross-coupling reactions catalyzed by metals such as Fe in particular.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fürstner|first1=Alois|last2=Leitner|first2=Andreas|last3=Méndez|first3=María|last4=Krause|first4=Helga|date=2002-11-01|title=Iron-Catalyzed Cross-Coupling Reactions|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=124|issue=46|pages=13856–13863|doi=10.1021/ja027190t|pmid=12431116|bibcode=2002JAChS.12413856F |issn=0002-7863}}</ref> His research in organometallic chemistry emphasized the importance of electron-transfer processes and radical species as intermediates.  Many of these results (and the results of other investigators) are summarized in a monograph.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Organometallic Mechanisms and Catalysis: The Role of Reactive Intermediates in Organic Processes|last=Kochi|first=Jay K.|publisher=Academic Press|year=1978|isbn=978-0-12-418250-9|location=New York}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Kochi received many awards for his research, including election to the U.S. [[National Academy of Sciences]]. He developed the [[Kochi reaction]], a variation on the [[Hunsdiecker reaction]].<ref>{{cite journal|title = A New Method for Halodecarboxylation of Acids Using Lead(IV) Acetate|first = Jay K.|last = Kochi|journal = [[Journal of the American Chemical Society]]|year = 1965|volume = 87|issue = 11|pages = 2500–2502|doi = 10.1021/ja01089a041 | bibcode=1965JAChS..87.2500K }}</ref>

==Personal life==
Kochi was of Japanese descent and he and his family were forcibly [[Internment of Japanese Americans|interned]] at the [[Gila River War Relocation Center]] during World War II.<ref name=inmemoriam>{{Cite journal |doi=10.1080/02603590802518644 |title=In Memoriam-Jay K. Kochi (1927–2008) |journal=Comments on Inorganic Chemistry |volume=29 |issue=5–6 |pages=130–131 |year=2008 |author1-link=John P. Fackler Jr. |last1=Fackler |first1=J. P. |s2cid=93238263 }}</ref><ref name=archives>{{cite web |title=Japanese American Internee Data File: Kazuo Kochi |url=https://aad.archives.gov/aad/record-detail.jsp?dt=3099&mtch=24&tf=F&q=Kochi&bc=&sort=30012%20desc&rpp=50&pg=1&rid=36306&rlst=36316,36300,36312,36314,36315,36303,36313,36306,36304,36317 | publisher=[[National Archives and Records Administration]]| access-date=August 18, 2019}}</ref> He died at his home in Houston, Texas on August 9, 2008, after a brief illness.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.isualum.org/s/565/17/interior.aspx?pgid=2929&gid=1 |title=Obituaries |work=Iowa State University Alumni Association}}</ref>
